The Proistamenos intones "Make firm, O Lord God, the holy Orthodox faith," the Priest gives the Sunday dismissal, and the faithful kiss the hand of the celebrant and receive the antidoron (*ἀντίδωρον*).

[^139]: The Ecclesiastical New Year (Indiction), September 1, St. Simeon the Stylite, and the Synaxis of the Theotokos of Miasena (Violakis, pp. 148–149, September 1, §1). The opening of the Fixed Cycle of the Menaion on September 1 marks the Byzantine Ecclesiastical New Year, designated the Indiction (*Ἀρχὴ τῆς Ἰνδίκτου*, Latin *Indictio*). The term originally designated the fifteen-year imperial Roman and Byzantine fiscal tax assessment cycle established under Emperor Constantine the Great, fixed to September 1 in 312 AD, and later codified as the official civil and ecclesiastical calendar beginning under Emperor Justinian I in 537 AD (Novella 47). In Christian typological theology, September 1 sanctifies the passage of cosmic time, commemorating Christ's inauguration of His public ministry in the synagogue of Nazareth (Luke 4:16–22) when He unrolled the scroll of the Prophet Isaiah and proclaimed "the acceptable year of the Lord" (Isaiah 61:1–2). Concurrently, the Church commemorates the venerable father St. Simeon the Stylite the Elder (c. 390–459 AD), who introduced the ascetic discipline of pillar-dwelling (stylitism) atop a column near Antioch, together with his mother St. Martha; as well as the Synaxis of the Most Holy Mother of God of Miasena (*Μιασηνῶν*), commemorating the miraculous discovery in the ninth century of her wonderworking icon, which had been cast into Lake Miasena in Armenia to preserve it from iconoclastic destruction during the reign of Emperor Leo the Isaurian. On weekdays, Great Vespers features the First Stasis of the First Kathisma of the Psalter (*Blessed is the man*, Psalm 1 LXX), ten Stichira at "Lord, I have cried" (three Prosomia of the Indiction, three of St. Simeon, and four Idiomela of the Indiction), festive Old Testament readings from Leviticus, Isaiah, and Wisdom, and concluding Dismissal Troparia: the Troparion of the Indiction, "O Creator of the universe, Who hast set the times and seasons in Thine own power..." (*Ὁ πάσης δημιουργός*, Tone 2); the Troparion of St. Simeon, "Thou didst become a pillar of endurance, O venerable one..." (*Ὑπομονῆς στῦλος*, Tone 1); and the Theotokion "Hail, full of grace, O Virgin Theotokos..." (*Χαῖρε κεχαριτωμένη*).

[^140]: Weekday Matins & Liturgy of the Indiction, Katavasiai of the Holy Cross, and Sunday Vespers Concurrence (Violakis, pp. 150–151, September 1, §§2–5). At Matins of the Indiction on a weekday, following the Midnight Office and the Hexapsalmos, the Troparia are chanted at "God is the Lord" as at Vespers. The hymnography includes two canons: the Canon of the Indiction (composed by St. John of Damascus, Tone 3) and the Canon of St. Simeon Stylites (Tone 2). A liturgical milestone occurs at the Katavasiai: beginning on September 1, the Church appoints the Katavasiai of the Universal Exaltation of the Precious and Life-Creating Cross: "Moses, having etched the cross with his rod, divided the Red Sea for Israel walking on foot..." (*Σταυρὸν χαράξας Μωσῆς*, Tone 8). These Katavasiai are chanted continuously through the Apodosis of the Exaltation on September 21. At the Divine Liturgy on weekdays, the Typika and Beatitudes incorporate troparia from Odes 3 and 6 of the Indiction Canon, followed by the Epistle (1 Tim. 2:1–7) and Gospel (Luke 4:16–22) of the Indiction, and the proper Communion Verse (Psalm 64:12 LXX): "Bless the crown of the year with Thy goodness, O Lord" (*Εὐλόγησον τὸν στέφανον τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ τῆς χρηστότητός σου, Κύριε*). When September 1 coincides with the Lord's Day (§§4–5), the Resurrectional service of the Octoechos joins with the Indiction: at Saturday Great Vespers, four Resurrection Stichira, three of the Indiction, and three of the Saint are chanted at "Lord, I have cried", crowned by the Indiction Doxastikon: "O Holy Spirit, Who art bound together with the Father and the Son in eternal timelessness..." (*Ὁ πνεύματι ἁγίῳ*), and the First Dogmatic Theotokion of the Tone.

[^141]: Sunday Concurrence of the Indiction, the Sunday before the Exaltation, and the Miracle of Archangel Michael at Chonae (Violakis, pp. 152–153, September 1 §6 & September 6 §§1–2). When September 1 falls on a Sunday, the Divine Liturgy appoints the Beatitudes divided four of the Resurrection Tone and four of Ode 6 of the Indiction Canon. Following the Little Entrance, the Dismissal Troparia are: the Resurrection Troparion, the Troparion of the Indiction, the Theotokion "Hail, full of grace", the Troparion of St. Simeon, and the Patron Saint of the temple, sealed by the Indiction Kontakion. Violakis records a critical calendar rule regarding the Saturday Indiction: if September 1 falls on a Saturday, the immediately subsequent Sunday is September 2; thus, on the following Sunday (which falls on September 8, or September 7 if an inclusive count was loosely used), the Epistle (Gal. 6:11–18) and Gospel (John 3:13–17) are appointed for the "Sunday before the Exaltation" (*Κυριακὴ πρὸ τῆς Ὑψώσεως*). On September 6, the Church commemorates the Miracle of the Archangel Michael at Colossae in Phrygia (Chonae) (*Τὸ ἐν Χώναις θαῦμα τοῦ Ἀρχιστρατήγου Μιχαήλ*), where the Archangel struck a great rock with his staff to open a subterranean chasm, swallowing two rushing torrents (the Lykokapros and Kouphos) diverted by pagans to submerge the sanctuary of the Archangel and destroy the hermit St. Archippus. When this feast falls on Sunday, Saturday Vespers joins six Resurrection Stichira with four of the Archangel, with the festal Doxastikon "Rejoice with us, all ye angelic ranks" (*Συγχάρητε ἡμῖν, ἅπασαι αἱ τῶν ἀγγέλων ταξιαρχίαι*), and the Dismissal Troparion of the Bodiless Powers: "Supreme commander of the heavenly hosts, we implore thee..." (*Τῶν οὐρανίων στρατιῶν Ἀρχιστράτηγε*, Tone 4).

[^142]: The Forefeast of the Nativity of the Theotokos and the Holy Martyr Sozon (Violakis, pp. 154–155, September 7, §§1–3). September 7 commemorates the Forefeast (*Προεόρτια*) of the Nativity of the Most Holy Mother of God, joined with the commemoration of the Holy Martyr Sozon of Lycaonia/Cilicia (martyred c. 304 AD under Maximian). When September 7 occurs on the Lord's Day, it coincides with the Sunday before the Exaltation. At Saturday Great Vespers, ten Stichira are chanted at "Lord, I have cried": six of the Resurrection and four Forefeast Idiomela, followed by the Forefeast Doxastikon: "Thy most venerable Nativity, O all-holy Virgin, pure Mother of God, the multitude of angels in heaven and the race of men upon earth do glorify..." (*Τὴν πάνσεπτόν σου Γέννησιν*), and the First Dogmatic Theotokion of the Tone. At the Aposticha, the Resurrection Stichira are concluded by the Forefeast Doxastikon: "The universal joy hath shone forth upon us from the righteous ones, Joachim and Anna..." (*Ἡ παγκόσμιος χαρά*), and the Dismissal Troparia: the Resurrection Troparion and the Forefeast Troparion: "From the root of Jesse and from the loins of David, Mary the child of God is born unto us today..." (*Ἐκ τῆς ῥίζης Ἰεσσαί*, Tone 4). Violakis notes that the hymnography of the Martyr Sozon is ordinarily relegated to Small Compline; however, if the local temple or parish observes his feast, three stichira of the Saint are intercalated at "Lord, I have cried" and his Troparion is added. At Sunday Matins, two Resurrection Kathismata and one Forefeast Kathisma are sung at each of the two Psalter stichologia. The Canons unite the Sunday Canon and the Forefeast Canon (with the refrain "Most Holy Theotokos, save us"), punctuated by the Katavasiai of the Cross. At the Liturgy, the readings are taken from the Sunday before the Exaltation (Gal. 6:11–18; John 3:13–17).


## Cohort 18 Footnotes

[^143]: The Nativity of the Most Holy Mother of God, September 8: Festal Rank, Vigil, and Typikon Synthesis (Violakis, pp. 156–157, September 8, §§4–5). The Nativity of the Most Holy Theotokos (*Τὸ Γενέσιον τῆς Ὑπεραγίας Θεοτόκου*) on September 8 is the first of the Twelve Great Feasts of the Byzantine ecclesiastical liturgical year, commemorating the birth of the Virgin Mary to the righteous ancestors of God Joachim and Anna in fulfillment of ancestral prophecies. Under the patriarchal reform of George Violakis, the feast is ranked among the great feasts of the Mother of God celebrated with Great Vespers, Litē (*Λιτή*), and festive Matins. When celebrated on a weekday, Great Vespers appoints the First Stasis of the First Kathisma of the Psalter (*Blessed is the man*, Psalm 1 LXX), followed at "Lord, I have cried" by six Idiomela Stichira in Tone 6 composed by St. Sergius of Jerusalem and St. Stephen the Sabaite, doubled with "Glory... Both now...". The three Old Testament lessons (Genesis 28:10–17, Jacob's ladder; Ezekiel 43:27–44:4, the shut gate seen by the prophet; Proverbs 9:1–11, Wisdom hath builded Her house) provide the primary typological framework for Marian veneration in the Byzantine rite. At Matins, the celebration incorporates the Midnight Office, the Festal Litē, and the Polyeleos taken from Psalm 44 LXX (*Ἐξηρεύξατο ἡ καρδία μου λόγον ἀγαθόν*, "My heart overfloweth with a good word"), which constitutes the royal epithalamium typifying the Mother of God as the Queen seated at the King's right hand. Following the Anavathmoi (Tone 4, Antiphon 1) and the Prokeimenon (Psalm 44:18 LXX), the Matins Gospel is Luke 1:39–49, 56 (the Visitation of Mary to Elizabeth and the Magnificat), followed by the post-Gospel Idiomelon in Tone 2 (*Αὕτη ἡ ἡμέρα Κυρίου*). The hymnography features two canons: the First Canon composed by St. John of Damascus (Tone 2, Heirmos: *Δεῦτε λαοί*) and the Second Canon composed by St. Andrew of Crete (Tone 8, Heirmos: *Ἁρματηλάτην Φαραώ*), punctuated by the Katavasiai of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross (*Σταυρὸν χαράξας*). At Ode 9, the biblical canticles give way to the proper festal megalynaria and the Ninth Ode Heirmos (*Μυστικὸς εἶ Θεοτόκε*).

[^144]: The Divine Liturgy of the Nativity of the Theotokos: Proper Festal Antiphons and Zadostoinyk (Violakis, pp. 158–159, September 8, §6). On the Feast of the Nativity of the Theotokos, the Divine Liturgy replaces the ordinary weekday psalms and Typika with three proper Festal Antiphons derived primarily from Psalm 131 LXX and Psalm 45 LXX. The first antiphon incorporates verses emphasizing David's vow to build a sanctuary for God (Psalm 131:1, 6; Psalm 86:3; Psalm 45:6 LXX) with the Marian refrain: "Through the intercessions of the Theotokos, O Savior, save us." The second antiphon presents the messianic oath made unto David regarding the royal heir to his eternal throne (Psalm 131:11, 17, 13 LXX) with the christological refrain: "Save us, O Son of God, Who art wonderful in the saints, who sing unto Thee: Alleluia!" (which in Ruthenian and Slavic practice is alternatively rendered: "Who art wonderful in the saints" or "Through the prayers of the Theotokos"). The third antiphon proclaims the eternal habitation of God in Sion (Psalm 131:14; Psalm 45:5; Psalm 64:5 LXX), interspersed with the festal Dismissal Troparion: "Thy Nativity, O Theotokos Virgin..." (*Ἡ γέννησίς σου Θεοτόκε*, Tone 4). At the Little Entrance, the clergy and choirs chant the festal Entrance Verse: "O come, let us worship and bow down before Christ: Save us, O Son of God, Who art wonderful in the saints, who sing unto Thee: Alleluia!". In place of the ordinary Marian hymn *Axion Estin*, the Liturgy appoints the Zadostoinyk (*Ἀντὶ τοῦ Ἄξιόν ἐστιν*), consisting of the festal megalynarion and the Heirmos of the Ninth Ode of the Second Canon (Tone 8): "Virginity is foreign to mothers, and childbearing strange to virgins; yet in thee, O Theotokos, both were accomplished: wherefore all we generations of the earth unceasingly magnify thee" (*Ἀλλότριον τῶν μητέρων ἡ παρθενία*). The Communion Verse is Psalm 115:4 LXX: "I will take the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord. Alleluia" (*Ποτήριον σωτηρίου λήψομαι*).

[^145]: Sunday Concurrence with the Nativity of the Theotokos and Precedence of the Sunday before the Exaltation (Violakis, pp. 160–161, September 8, §§7–9). When September 8 falls on the Lord's Day, a complex liturgical concurrence occurs between the Resurrectional service of the prevailing Octoechos Tone, the Feast of the Nativity of the Theotokos, and the Sunday before the Exaltation of the Precious Cross (*Κυριακὴ πρὸ τῆς Ὑψώσεως*). At Saturday Great Vespers, the ten Stichira at "Lord, I have cried" are divided: four of the Resurrection and six Idiomela of the Feast, with the festal Doxastikon (*Σήμερον ὁ τοῖς νοεροῖς θρόνοις*) chanted at "Glory... Both now...". The Old Testament readings of the Feast are retained. At the Aposticha, the Resurrection Stichira take precedence, concluded by the festal Doxastikon: "Come, all ye faithful" (*Δεῦτε ἅπαντες πιστοί*). At Matins, the Polyeleos of the Feast is appended to the Psalter Kathismata, and the Sunday Anavathmoi are followed by the festal Prokeimenon and the festal Matins Gospel (Luke 1:39–49, 56). The Sunday chant *Anastasin Christou theasamenoi* is sung, followed by the festal Idiomelon at Psalm 50. In the hymnographic canon, the Resurrection Canon precedes both Canons of the Feast, and the Katavasiai remain those of the Precious Cross (*Σταυρὸν χαράξας*). At the Divine Liturgy, the proper Festal Antiphons are sung with the Sunday second-antiphon refrain: "Save us, O Son of God, Who art risen from the dead...". Crucially, Violakis specifies that the Epistle (Galatians 6:11–18: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ") and the Gospel (John 3:13–17: "No man hath ascended up to heaven, but He that came down from heaven...") are taken exclusively from the Sunday before the Exaltation, while the Zadostoinyk and Communion Verse remain those of the Nativity of the Theotokos.

[^146]: Commemoration of the Holy and Righteous Ancestors of God Joachim and Anna on Sunday and Afterfeast Progression (Violakis, pp. 162–163, September 9, §§10–13). September 9 observes the Synaxis of the Holy and Righteous Ancestors of God Joachim and Anna (*Σύναξις τῶν ἁγίων καὶ δικαίων Θεοπατόρων Ἰωακεὶμ καὶ Ἄννης*), celebrating the parents of the Mother of God on the day following her Nativity, according to the ancient patristic principle whereby the primary human instruments of a divine mystery are venerated on the morrow of the feast. On weekdays, their office is joined directly with the hymns of the Afterfeast from the Menaion. When September 9 coincides with Sunday (§§10–12), the service of the Lord's Day combines six Resurrection Stichira with four of the Ancestors of God (*Δεῦτε νῦν χορεύσωμεν*), crowned by their Doxastikon: "O blessed couple, Joachim and Anna" (*Ὦ μακαρία δυάς*), and the First Dogmatic Theotokion of the Tone. At the Aposticha, the Resurrection Stichira are sealed by the Doxastikon of the Saints: "They who from barren loins" (*Οἱ ἐξ ἀκάρπων λαγόνων*), and the Dismissal Troparia include the Resurrection Troparion, the Troparion of the Saints (*Οἱ ἐν χάριτι δικαιωθέντες* or their proper dismissal troparion), and the festal Troparion of the Nativity. At Matins, the Kathismata of the Feast replace the ordinary Theotokia, and the Canons join the Resurrection Canon with the Canon of the Saints, sealed by the Katavasiai of the Cross. At the Liturgy, the Beatitudes combine four of the Tone and four from Ode 6 of the Canon of the Saints, and the readings are those of the Sunday before the Exaltation. Paragraph 13 establishes the general rubric for the "Sunday after the Feast" (*Κυριακὴ μετὰ τὴν ἑορτήν*), when the Afterfeast continues through September 12.

[^147]: The Apodosis of the Nativity of the Theotokos on Weekdays and Sunday (Violakis, pp. 164–165, September 12, §§15–17). The liturgical cycle of the Nativity of the Theotokos culminates on September 12 with its Apodosis (*Ἀπόδοσις*), concluding the four-day Afterfeast period prior to the inauguration of the Forefeast of the Universal Exaltation of the Precious Cross on September 13. When the Apodosis falls on a weekday (§15), the entire service of September 8 is repeated verbatim with specific omissions reflecting its non-initiatory character: at Vespers, the Kathisma of the Psalter and the three Old Testament readings are omitted; at Matins, the Litē, the Polyeleos, and the festal Matins Gospel are omitted, while the full festal canons, Katavasiai, and praises are sung; at the Divine Liturgy, the festal antiphons and Zadostoinyk are repeated, but the Epistle and Gospel are appointed from the regular weekday cycle. When the Apodosis coincides with Sunday (§§16–17), it merges with the Sunday before the Exaltation. At Saturday Great Vespers, four Resurrection Stichira combine with six of the Feast, and the Aposticha join the Resurrection stichira with the festal aposticha. At Sunday Matins, the Resurrection Kathismata are intercalated with those of the Feast, the Canons combine the Resurrection and the Feast, and the Katavasiai of the Cross are chanted. The Liturgy unites the Sunday Beatitudes with Ode 6 of the Feast, the Epistle and Gospel of the Sunday before the Exaltation, and the Zadostoinyk and festal Communion Verse of the Nativity.


## Cohort 19 Footnotes

[^148]: Feast of the Consecration of the Temple of the Holy Resurrection in Jerusalem and Forefeast of the Holy Cross on Sunday (Violakis, pp. 166–169, September 13, §§1–4). September 13 commemorates the Dedication or Consecration (*Ἐγκαίνια*) of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre (the Temple of the Resurrection, *Ἀνάστασις*) in Jerusalem, constructed under the Emperor Saint Constantine the Great and consecrated in A.D. 335. In Byzantine liturgical theology, this feast serves as the historical and liturgical threshold for the Universal Exaltation of the Precious and Life-Creating Cross on the following day (September 14), since the Holy Cross was first solemnly displayed and exalted before the assembled Christian multitude on the morrow of this very consecration. The day is also observed as the Forefeast (*Προεόρτια*) of the Precious Cross and commemorates the Holy Hieromartyr Cornelius the Centurion. When September 13 concurs with the Lord's Day (§§2–4), the office combines the Sunday Resurrectional order with the festal propers of the Consecration and the Forefeast. At Saturday Great Vespers, the ten Stichira at "Lord, I have cried" are partitioned into four of the Resurrection, three of the Consecration, and three of the Forefeast taken from Small Vespers (*Ὑψουμένου σου Δέσποτα*), crowned by the Doxastikon of the Consecration (*Τὴν μνήμην τῶν Ἐγκαινίων*) and the First Dogmatic Theotokion of the Tone. The Old Testament readings of the Consecration (1 Kings 8:22–30, the dedication prayer of Solomon; Proverbs 3:19–34, the establishment of the earth by Wisdom; Proverbs 9:1–11, Wisdom hath builded Her house) reflect the christological fulfillment of the temple in the Body of Christ and the Church. At Matins, the Triadic Canon and hymns precede the dismissal troparia: the Resurrection Troparion, the Troparion of the Consecration (*Ὡς τοῦ ἄνω στερεώματος*), and the Forefeast Troparion (*Τὸν ζωοποιὸν Σταυρὸν τῆς σῆς ἀγαθότητος*). The hymnographic canon combines the Resurrection Canon with the Canon of the Cross (Tone 4, by St. Cosmas of Maiuma) and the Canon of the Consecration (Tone 4, by St. John of Damascus), punctuated by the Katavasiai of the Holy Cross (*Σταυρὸν χαράξας*). At the Divine Liturgy, the Beatitudes combine four of the Tone with four from Ode 6 of the Canon of the Consecration; the Epistle (Galatians 6:11–18) and Gospel (John 3:13–17) are taken from the Sunday before the Exaltation, while the Zadostoinyk remains the ordinary *Axion Estin*.

[^149]: Translation and Commemoration of St. John Chrysostom on the Feast of the Universal Exaltation of the Precious Cross (Violakis, pp. 168–169, September 14, Rubrical Note). Historically, Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople and Doctor of the Universal Church, fell asleep in the Lord on September 14, A.D. 407, at Comana in Pontus during his second exile. Because September 14 is dedicated entirely to the Universal Exaltation of the Precious and Life-Creating Cross—a feast ranking as a Great Feast of the Lord which completely absorbs all other commemorations—the liturgical constitution of the Byzantine rite transfers the liturgical celebration of Saint John Chrysostom to November 13. The rubrical note in the Violakis Typikon explicitly records that this transfer was instituted precisely so that the hymns, readings, and liturgical praises of Saint John Chrysostom might remain complete, intact, and undiminished (*ἀνελλιπῆ καὶ ἀμείωτα*), without being displaced or curtailed by the festal hegemony of the Exaltation. This principle reflects the traditional Byzantine typikon jurisprudence regarding feast day displacement and ensures the full commemoration of both the Precious Cross and the universal hierarch.

[^150]: Sunday Precedence, Festal Absorption, and the Liturgical Rite of the Procession of the Holy Cross at Matins (Violakis, pp. 170–171, September 14, §§5–6). The Universal Exaltation of the Precious and Life-Creating Cross on September 14 constitutes one of the Twelve Great Feasts of the Lord (*Δεσποτικαὶ ἑορταί*). When September 14 coincides with the Lord's Day (§5), an exceptional rule of festal absorption governs the services: the entire Sunday Resurrectional office is superseded and eliminated, and the festal propers of the Holy Cross are chanted exclusively (*οὐδὲν τῶν Ἀναστασίμων ψάλλομεν, ἀλλ’ ἅπαντα τὰ τῆς ἑορτῆς*). Only two elements of Sunday character are retained: the chant *Anastasin Christou theasamenoi* ("Having beheld the Resurrection of Christ") at Matins, which is uniquely appointed to be chanted on the Exaltation regardless of the day of the week on which the feast falls, signifying the indissoluble bond between the Cross and the Resurrection; and the Matins Gospel reading (John 12:28–36), read from the Royal Doors. At the conclusion of the Great Doxology, during the slow and ornate chanting of the Asmatikon Trisagion (*Ἅγιος ὁ Θεός*), the solemn liturgical Procession of the Precious Cross takes place. The officiating priest, having censed the Cross on the Holy Table where it rests on a tray amidst sprigs of sweet basil and three lighted candles, lifts the tray upon his head. Preceded by lighted tapers, the six-winged liturgical fans (*Exapteryga*), the chanters, and the Primikyrios bearing the two-wicked candle (*Didamvulon*), the priest circles the Holy Table from right to left (counter-clockwise) and carries the Cross through the Holy Doors to the center of the temple. There, circling the adorned Tetrapod three times, he stops facing East, elevates the tray, proclaims the liturgical cry *Sophia, orthoi!* ("Wisdom! Let us attend!"), and deposits the Cross upon the Tetrapod for the ceremony of the Elevation.

[^151]: The Solemn Rite of the Fivefold Elevation of the Holy Cross with Five Hundred Kyrie Eleisons (Violakis, pp. 172–173, September 14, §6 continued). The ceremonial pinnacle of the feast of the Exaltation is the Fivefold Elevation (*Ὕψωσις*) of the Precious Cross, historically commemorating both the recovery of the Cross by Saint Helen in A.D. 326 and its recovery from the Persians by Emperor Heraclius in A.D. 628, followed by its solemn elevation by Patriarch Macarius and Patriarch Zacharias before the weeping and rejoicing faithful. The liturgical rite prescribed in the Violakis Typikon preserves the ancient Constantinopolitan patriarchal cathedral ritual: After the priest censes the Cross on the Tetrapod from all four sides and the Dismissal Troparion (*Σῶσον, Κύριε, τὸν λαόν σου*) is sung thrice, the priest makes three prostrations, lifts the Cross adorned with basil, and facing East proclaims the First Petition of the Insistent Litany (*Ἐλέησον ἡμᾶς, ὁ Θεός*). While the choirs chant one hundred *Kyrie eleisons*, the priest signs thrice with the Cross, slowly bows his body until his head is one span from the earth, and then slowly straightens until he stands erect as the hundredth chant concludes. He then turns successively to the remaining quarters of the world to execute the remaining four Elevations: the Second Elevation facing North for all pious Orthodox Christians; the Third Elevation facing West for the ruling Patriarch and Hierarchs; the Fourth Elevation facing South for the absent bishops and dioceses; and the Fifth Elevation facing East for all clergy, benefactors, and the salvation of all Orthodox souls. Across the five elevations, five hundred *Kyrie eleisons* are chanted, symbolizing the total consecration and cosmic sanctification of the four corners of the world through the power of the Wood of the Cross. Following the elevations, the Patriarch or bishop ascends the dais, elevates the Cross with the Kontakion *Ὁ ὑψωθεὶς ἐν τῷ Σταυρῷ*, and leads the clergy and faithful in the adoration hymn: *Τὸν Σταυρόν σου προσκυνοῦμεν, Δέσποτα* ("We venerate Thy Cross, O Master"), followed by the distribution of the sanctified basil sprigs.

[^152]: The Festal Antiphons of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross and Non-Hierarchical Parish Rubrics (Violakis, pp. 174–175, September 14, §7 and Rubrical Note). The rubrical note on page 174 provides the essential canonical differentiation between cathedral celebrations presided over by the Patriarch or an active bishop and celebrations in ordinary parish or monastic churches served by a priest alone. In the absence of a bishop, the single priest executes the fivefold elevation unassisted, modifying the fourth petition to intercede directly for the parish wardens (*Ἐπίτροποι*), parish community, and benefactors. At the Divine Liturgy (§7), the standard Sunday or weekday Typika psalms are entirely replaced by the three proper Festal Antiphons of the Exaltation, drawn from the messianic and cruciform verses of the Septuagint Psalter: Antiphon 1 is taken from Psalm 21 LXX (*Ὁ Θεός, ὁ Θεός μου, πρόσχες μοι*), the prophetic psalm of the Passion of the Messiah, chanted with the Marian refrain *Taîs presveíais tês Theotókou*; Antiphon 2 is derived from Psalm 73 LXX (*Ἵνα τί, ὁ Θεός, ἀπώσω εἰς τέλος;*), which recounts the affliction of the sanctuary and confesses God as the eternal King Who wrought salvation upon the earth, chanted with the invariable christological refrain: *Σῶσον ἡμᾶς, Υἱὲ Θεοῦ, ὁ σαρκὶ σταυρωθείς, ψάλλοντάς σοι· Ἀλληλούϊα* ("Save us, O Son of God, Who wast crucified in the flesh, who sing unto Thee: Alleluia"), which is sung on the feast regardless of the day of the week; Antiphon 3 is taken from Psalm 98 LXX (*Ὁ Κύριος ἐβασίλευσεν, ὀργιζέσθωσαν λαοί*), proclaiming the divine sovereignty and the exaltation of His footstool, interspersed with the festal Dismissal Troparion: *Σῶσον, Κύριε, τὸν λαόν σου*. The critical footnote on page 174 records an erratum of the first printed edition of the Violakis Typikon, which accidentally omitted the rubric header for Antiphon 3 in Tone 1, restored by the liturgical redactor through concordance with the authoritative Constantinopolitan Menaion.


## Cohort 20 Footnotes

[^153]: Strict Fast Discipline, Equal Rank to Great Friday, and Concluding Liturgical Propers of the Universal Exaltation of the Precious Cross (Violakis, pp. 176–177, September 14, §7 concl., Rubrical Notes, and September Saturday after Exaltation, §8). The rubrical constitution of the Byzantine rite elevates the Feast of the Universal Exaltation of the Precious and Life-Creating Cross to an exceptional ascetical standing: it is explicitly designated as “bearing the equal rank of Holy and Great Friday” (*φερούσῃ τὰ ἴσα τῆς ἁγίας καὶ Μ. Παρασκευῆς*). Consequently, a strict total fast (*νηστεία*) is canonically enjoined upon the entire body of the Church on September 14 regardless of the day of the week on which it falls, excluding all flesh-meat, dairy products, eggs, and fish. In accordance with Apostolic Canon 64 and the ancient canonical tradition that forbids strict fasting (xerophagy) on the Sabbath or the Lord's Day, an ascetical relaxation or dispensation (*κατάλυσις*) for wine and olive oil is permitted only when September 14 concurs with a Saturday or a Sunday. At Vespers on the evening of the Feast, the Great Prokeimenon *Ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ καὶ ἐν τῇ γῇ* (“Our God is in heaven and on earth: all things whatsoever He willed, He hath done”, Psalm 113:11 LXX) is solemnly chanted with its verses, an invariable mark of Great Feasts of the Lord. The concluding propers of the Divine Liturgy (§7 concl.) mirror the high festal dignity of the Cross: The proper Festal Isodikon (*Ὑψοῦτε Κύριον τὸν Θεὸν ἡμῶν*, Psalm 98:5 LXX) incorporates the proper christological refrain *Σῶσον ἡμᾶς, Υἱὲ Θεοῦ, ὁ σαρκὶ σταυρωθείς*; the Trisagion is replaced by the hymn of solemn adoration *Τὸν Σταυρόν σου προσκυνοῦμεν, Δέσποτα, καὶ τὴν ἁγίαν σου Ἀνάστασιν δοξάζομεν* (“We venerate Thy Cross, O Master, and we glorify Thy holy Resurrection”); the festive Epistle pericope (1 Corinthians 1:18–24: “For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God”) and Gospel reading (John 19:6–11, 13–20, 25–28, 30–35, the solemn Passion account of the Crucifixion) bear witness to the salvific triumph of Golgotha; the festal Megalynarion [Zadostoinyk] is the Heirmos of Ode 9 of the First Canon of the Cross: *Μυστικὸς εἶ, Θεοτόκε, παράδεισος* (“O Theotokos, Thou art a mystical paradise”, Tone 8); and the Communion Verse is Psalm 4:7 LXX (*Ἐσημειώθη ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς τὸ φῶς τοῦ προσώπου σου, Κύριε*). At §8, the order for the Saturday after the Exaltation (*Σαββάτῳ μετὰ τὴν Ὕψωσιν*) establishes the post-festal weekday structure: the Canons of the Feast and of the occurring Saint are recited in direct sequence (*χῦμα*), the Magnificat (*Τὴν τιμιωτέραν*) is chanted, the festal Antiphons and Entrance Hymn are maintained at the Divine Liturgy, and the appointed scriptural readings are 1 Corinthians 1:26–29 and John 8:21–30.

[^154]: Sunday after the Universal Exaltation of the Precious Cross and Concurrence with the Great-Martyr Euphemia (Violakis, pp. 178–179, September Sunday after Exaltation, §§9–11, and September 16, §§12–14). The Sunday after the Exaltation (*Κυριακὴ μετὰ τὴν Ὕψωσιν*, §§9–11) holds a primary structural position within the autumnal post-festal cycle of the Byzantine Menologion. While the ordinary Sunday Resurrectional order reasserts its primacy over the liturgical structure (governing the Tone of the week, the Resurrection Stichira, the Sunday Evlogitaria, the Sunday Morning Gospel, and the Great Doxology dismissal troparion *Σήμερον σωτηρία*), the post-festal presence of the Holy Cross permeates every service. At Saturday Great Vespers (§9), 6 Resurrection Stichira are joined to 4 post-festal Stichira of the Cross, crowned by the festal Doxastikon. At Sunday Matins (§10), both the Resurrection Canon and the Canon of the Cross are chanted, accompanied by the Katavasiai *Σταυρὸν χαράξας*. At the Divine Liturgy (§11), the Beatitudes combine four of the Tone with four from Ode 6 of the Canon of the Feast, and the scriptural pericopes provide the theological core of the post-festal season: the Epistle pericope (Galatians 2:16–20: “I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me”) and the Gospel pericope (Mark 8:34–9:1: “Whosoever will come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow Me”). At §§12–14, the Typikon addresses the concurrence of the Holy Glorious Great-Martyr and All-Praised Euphemia (September 16). Although Saint Euphemia was martyred under Diocletian at Chalcedon (A.D. 304), her liturgical office is especially renowned for the Miracle of the Fourth Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon (A.D. 451), commemorated on July 11, in which the rival Tomes of the Orthodox and the Monophysites were placed in her reliquary, and upon reopening, the Orthodox Tome of Pope Saint Leo was found held in her right hand while the heretical Tome was cast at her feet. When her feast falls on Sunday within the afterfeast of the Cross (§§13–14), the ten Stichira at “Lord, I have cried” are partitioned into 4 Resurrection, 3 post-festal of the Cross, and 3 of the Saint, with the Doxastikon assigned to Saint Euphemia (*Ἡ διηνθισμένη ταῖς ἀρεταῖς*) and “Both now” to the First Dogmatic Theotokion of the Tone; at Matins, three canons are chanted (Resurrection, Cross, and Saint Euphemia), and the Kathisma of the Saint is sung after Ode 3.

[^155]: Sunday Concurrence with the Holy Great-Martyr Eustathius and the Architecture of Post-Festal Weekday/Sunday Offices (Violakis, pp. 180–181, September 16 concl., §15, and September 20, §16). Section 15 concludes the Divine Liturgy for the Sunday concurrence of Saint Euphemia within the afterfeast: the Beatitudes combine 4 of the Tone with 4 from Ode 6 of the Canon of Saint Euphemia; following the Little Entrance, the dismissal troparia are sung in sequence (Resurrection, Feast of the Cross, Saint Euphemia, and the Patron Saint of the local temple), followed by the festal Kontakion *Ὁ ὑψωθεὶς ἐν τῷ Σταυρῷ*, while the Epistle and Gospel remain those of the Sunday after the Exaltation. Section 16 governs the feast of the Holy Great-Martyr Eustathius (Placidus), his wife Theopiste, and their sons Agapius and Theopistus (September 20), who suffered martyrdom by being enclosed in a heated bronze bull under Emperor Hadrian (c. A.D. 118). Falling on the penultimate day of the post-festal period of the Exaltation, the concurrence of Saint Eustathius on Sunday provides a canonical template for integrating a Polyeleos-rank Saint within an Afterfeast: at Saturday Great Vespers, the Stichira at “Lord, I have cried” are apportioned 4 of the Resurrection, 3 of the Afterfeast of the Cross, and 3 of Saint Eustathius; at the Aposticha, the Doxastikon is assigned to the Saint, followed by “Both now” and the post-festal Doxastikon of the Cross; the dismissal troparia consist of the Resurrection Troparion, that of Saint Eustathius (*Οἱ μάρτυρές σου, Κύριε*), and that of the Feast (*Σῶσον, Κύριε, τὸν λαόν σου*). At Matins, the three canons are combined (Resurrection, Cross, and Saint Eustathius), with the Kathisma of the Saint sung after Ode 3; at the Divine Liturgy, the troparia of the Resurrection, the Cross, Saint Eustathius, and the temple Patron Saint are chanted after the Little Entrance, crowned by the festal Kontakion *Ὁ ὑψωθεὶς ἐν τῷ Σταυρῷ*, while the Epistle and Gospel remain those of the Sunday after the Exaltation.

[^156]: The Apodosis (Leave-Taking) of the Universal Exaltation of the Precious Cross and the Autumnal Katavasia Transition (Violakis, pp. 182–183, September 21, §§17–20, and Rubrical Note). The Apodosis (*Ἀπόδοσις*) of the Universal Exaltation of the Precious Cross on September 21 (§§17–20) brings the eight-day post-festal cycle to its liturgical consummation. When falling on a weekday (§17), the service replicates the principal day of the feast in all its hymnography, with the rubrical omission of the Old Testament readings at Vespers and the festal additions at Matins (the Liti, the Matins Gospel, and the Polyeleos); at the Divine Liturgy, the daily Epistle and Gospel are read. When the Apodosis coincides with Sunday (§§18–20), the Sunday Resurrectional office and the festal Apodosis merge: Great Vespers (§18) appoints 4 Resurrection and 6 Festal Stichira at “Lord, I have cried”, while the Aposticha assigns both “Glory” and “Both now” to the Feast. At Sunday Matins (§19), the Resurrection Dismissal Troparion is chanted once and the Festal Troparion twice; the Resurrection Canon is combined with the Canon of the Cross, culminating in the solemn chanting of the Ninth Ode of the Feast with both of its Katavasiai (*Μυστικὸς εἶ, Θεοτόκε* and *Ὁ διὰ βρώσεως τοῦ ξύλου*). At the Divine Liturgy (§20), the proper Festal Antiphons are retained: at Antiphon 2, the refrain is *Ὁ σαρκὶ σταυρωθείς*; at the Little Entrance, the festal Isodikon combines the festal verse with the Sunday refrain *Ὁ ἀναστὰς ἐκ νεκρῶν*; and in place of *Axion Estin*, the festal Zadostoinyk is chanted: *Ὁ διὰ βρώσεως τοῦ ξύλου* (the Heirmos of Ode 9 of the Second Canon of the Cross by St. John of Damascus). The concluding rubrical note defines the structural boundary of the Menologion: beginning on the first Sunday after the Apodosis of the Cross, the appointed Katavasiai transition to the Marian canon *Ἀνοίξω τὸ στόμα μου* (“I shall open my mouth”, Tone 4) through November 21 (the Feast of the Entry of the Most Holy Theotokos into the Temple), while the seasonal Kontakion becomes *Προστασία τῶν Χριστιανῶν ἀκαταίσχυντε* (“O Protection of Christians that cannot be put to shame”, Tone 2) through November 8 (the Synaxis of the Archangel Michael and the Bodiless Hosts).

[^157]: The Conception of the Honorable Forerunner, Text-Critical Rectification of Stichira Count, and the Theotokos of Kythera with St. Thecla (Violakis, pp. 184–185, September 23, §§1–3, and September 24, §1). September 23 marks the Feast of the Conception of the Honorable and Glorious Prophet, Forerunner, and Baptist John (*Ἡ Σύλληψις τοῦ τιμίου Προδρόμου*, §§1–3), which celebrates the supernatural intervention of God in the conception of John by the elderly and barren Elizabeth following the angelic annunciation to the Priest Zacharias in the Holy of Holies (Luke 1:5–25). When this feast concurs with Sunday (§§2–3), Great Vespers appoints ten Stichira at “Lord, I have cried”. A significant text-critical divergence exists between the editio princeps of the Greek text and its original English facing page: the Greek text definitively specifies six Resurrection Stichira and four of the Forerunner (`Ἀναστάσιμα ς΄ καὶ τοῦ Προδρόμου δ΄`), completing the requisite decuple; the English translation facing leaf in the 1888 edition erroneously recorded “3 Stichira of the Forerunner”, which would have left the decuple incomplete with only nine Stichira. This critical edition rectifies the erratum in conformity with the primary Greek witness and the authoritative Constantinopolitan Menaion. At Matins (§3), the Kathisma *Θυμιῶντι ἐν Ναῷ* (“As Zacharias was offering incense in the temple”) and the Theotokion *Κατεπλάγη Ἰωσήφ* (“Joseph was struck with wonder”) follow Ode 3; at the Divine Liturgy, the Epistle is assigned to the Forerunner (Galatians 4:22–31, allegorizing the barren Sarah and the child of promise Isaac), while the Gospel is that of the Sunday. Section 1 of September 24 details the concurrence on Sunday of the Wonderworking Icon of the Most Holy Theotokos of Kythera (*Παναγία ἡ Μυρτιδιώτισσα*, “Our Lady of the Myrtle Tree”, commemorating the miraculous discovery of the holy icon amidst myrtle branches on the Aegean island of Kythera in the 14th century and the healing of a paralytic) with the Holy Protomartyr and Equal-of-the-Apostles Thecla of Iconium (first century), spiritual daughter and disciple of the Holy Apostle Paul.

[^159]: Feast of the Metastasis of Saint John the Theologian, Ceremonial Standing for Paremiae, and Folio Transition (Violakis, pp. 188–189, September 26, §§1–3 incipit). September 26 marks the solemn commemoration of the Falling Asleep (Metastasis) of the Holy, Glorious Apostle and Evangelist John the Theologian (*Ἡ μετάστασις τοῦ ἁγίου ἐνδόξου Ἀποστόλου καὶ Εὐαγγελιστοῦ Ἰωάννου τοῦ Θεολόγου*). At Great Vespers (§1), following the First Stasis of the First Kathisma of the Psalter (Psalms 1–3 LXX), three Prosomia are sung at "Lord, I have cried" doubled unto 6, followed by the Entrance with the censer (*Φῶς ἱλαρόν*) and the daily Prokeimenon. The three festal Old Testament readings (Paremiae) are unique in the Byzantine liturgical corpus: rather than being drawn from the Old Testament prophets or wisdom literature, they are excerpted from the New Testament Catholic Epistles of Saint John himself (1 John 3:21–4:6; 1 John 4:11–16; and 1 John 4:20–5:5). Because these readings derive from apostolic canonical Scripture, the Great Church of Constantinople prescribes an exceptional ceremonial rubric: *(καθ’ ἅ ἡμεῖς ἱστάμεθα, ὁ δὲ Διάκονος ἐκφωνεῖ Πρόσχωμεν, Σοφία, Πρόσχωμεν)* ("during which we stand upright, as the Deacon exclaims: Let us be attentive! Wisdom! Let us be attentive!"). This elevates the Paremiae to a liturgical honor normally reserved exclusively for the Holy Gospel and apostolic lections. At Matins (§2), the order includes the Liti, the Polyeleos, the First Antiphon of the Anavathmoi of Tone 4 (*Ἐκ νεότητός μου*), the festal Prokeimenon (Psalm 18:5 LXX: *Εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν*), and the Eleventh Morning Gospel (John 21:15–25, detailing Christ's dialogue with Peter regarding the beloved disciple). [^161]: The Tripartite Annual Commemoration of the Ecumenical Councils in the Constantinopolitan Typikon (Violakis, pp. 194–195, October 11–17, Concluding Rubrical Note). Appended to the rubric of the Seventh Ecumenical Council on printed page 194 is a fundamental didascalic note (*Σημείωσις*) summarizing the three annual corporate celebrations dedicated to the Holy Fathers of the Ecumenical Councils in the Byzantine liturgical year: (1) The First Ecumenical Council (Nicaea I, A.D. 325, which formulated the initial clauses of the Nicene Creed and anathematized Arius), commemorated on the Seventh Sunday of Pascha (the Sunday after the Ascension of our Lord), with the appointed Gospel pericope from Saint John (John 17:1–13, the High Priestly Prayer of Christ for the unity of the Church); (2) The Fourth Ecumenical Council (Chalcedon, A.D. 451, which confessed the two unconfused and undivided natures of Christ, celebrated jointly with the First Six Ecumenical Councils), commemorated on the Sunday falling between July 13 and 19 inclusive, with the appointed Gospel pericope from Saint Matthew (Matthew 5:14–19, "Ye are the light of the world... Whosoever shall do and teach them, the same shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven"); and (3) The Seventh Ecumenical Council (Nicaea II, A.D. 787, which restored the veneration of the holy icons), commemorated on the Sunday falling between October 11 and 17 inclusive, with the appointed Gospel pericope from Saint Luke (Luke 8:5–15, the Parable of the Sower, from the Fourth Sunday of Luke). This note provides liturgical coordinators and cantors with an authoritative comparative key to the three major patristic celebrations that anchor the movable and fixed cycles of the Constantinopolitan typikon.

[^164]: Commemoration of St. Artemios, St. Matrona of Chios, and St. Gerasimos of Cephalonia, Special Festal Booklets, and Sunday Concurrence (Violakis, pp. 196–199, October 20, §§ 1–4). October 20 unites the general Byzantine commemoration of the Holy Great-Martyr Artemios (beheaded under Julian the Apostate in A.D. 363) with two highly venerated post-Byzantine monastic saints whose offices developed in regional pamphlets (*ἰδιαίτεραι φυλλάδες*): the Righteous Mother Matrona of Chios (d. 1462, whose office was composed and popularized across the Aegean islands) and our Righteous Father Gerasimos the New Ascetic of Cephalonia (d. 1579, whose incorrupt relics in Omala form the monastic heart of the Ionian Islands). When October 20 falls on a weekday (§ 1), the first three Stichira at "Lord, I have cried" are sung for Saint Artemios from the general Menaion, followed by three Stichira for Saint Matrona or Saint Gerasimos from their respective booklets, with the Doxastikon assigned to whichever local patron is celebrated. When occurring on a Sunday (§§ 2–4), Saturday Great Vespers prescribes 4 Resurrection Stichira, 3 of Saint Artemios, and 3 of Saint Matrona or Saint Gerasimos; at Matins, the Liti is taken from the booklet of the righteous saint, followed by the Triadic hymns (*Ἄξιόν ἐστιν*) and the third Kathisma reading assigned to the saint; at the Divine Liturgy, the Beatitudes combine 4 of the Tone and 4 from Ode 6 of the Canon of the righteous saint, with the Epistle taken from the saint's office (Galatians 3:23–4:5 for a female ascetic or Galatians 5:22–6:2 for a venerable monk) and the Sunday Gospel.

[^165]: Feast of the Holy Apostle James, Brother of the Lord (Adelphotheos), Sunday Concurrence, and Apolytikion (Violakis, pp. 198–201, October 23, §§ 1–4). October 23 commemorates Saint James the Brother of the Lord (*Ἰάκωβος ὁ Ἀδελφόθεος*), first Bishop of Jerusalem, author of the Catholic Epistle of James, and martyr under the High Priest Ananus II in A.D. 62. On a weekday (§ 1), the office is sung plain from the Menaion. When the feast occurs on a Sunday (§§ 2–4), Great Vespers on Saturday evening appoints 6 Resurrection Stichira and 4 Stichira of the Apostle at "Lord, I have cried"; the Doxastikon is *Αἵματι τοῦ μαρτυρίου* ("With the blood of martyrdom"); at the Aposticha, the Doxastikon is *Τοῦ Ἀρχιποίμενος Χριστοῦ* ("Of Christ the Chief Shepherd"); and the Dismissal Troparion is the ancient troparion of Saint James: *Ὡς τοῦ Κυρίου μαθητὴς ἀνεδέξω, δίκαιε, τὸ Εὐαγγέλιον· ὡς μάρτυς ἔχεις τὸ ἀπαράτρεπτον· τὴν παρρησίαν ὡς ἀδελφόθεος· τὸ πρεσβεύειν ὡς ἱεράρχης* ("As a disciple of the Lord thou didst receive the Gospel, O righteous one; as a martyr thou hast that which cannot be changed; boldness as the Brother of God; and intercession as a hierarch"). At Matins (§ 3), after the Amomos (Psalm 118 LXX) and the Canons, the Katavasiai *Ἀνοίξω τὸ στόμα μου* are sung; at the Divine Liturgy (§ 4), the Beatitudes combine 4 of the Tone with 4 from Ode 6 of the Canon of the Apostle, the Epistle is Galatians 1:11–19 (Saint Paul recounting his apostolic calling and his meeting in Jerusalem with "James the Lord's brother"), and the Sunday Gospel is appointed.

[^166]: Feast of the Holy Great-Martyr Demetrios the Myrrh-Streamer and the Commemoration of the Great Earthquake at Constantinople (Violakis, pp. 200–205, October 26, §§ 1–8). October 26 is one of the most solemn feast days of the Byzantine calendar, combining the major martyrdom of Saint Demetrios of Thessalonica (martyred ca. A.D. 306 under Maximian Galerius) with the civil and liturgical commemoration of the cataclysmic earthquake that struck Constantinople on October 26, A.D. 740, under Emperor Leo III the Isaurian (the Violakis heading parenthetically cites 791, reflecting a recensional chronological discrepancy found in certain post-Byzantine liturgical printed synaxaria). At Vespers (§ 1), 6 festal Stichira of Saint Demetrios are sung at "Lord, I have cried", followed by three Old Testament lections (Prophecies: Isaiah 63:15–64:5, 8–9; Jeremiah 2:2–12; and Wisdom of Solomon 3:1–9); at the Aposticha, the penitential Idiomela of the Earthquake are sung, followed by the Doxastikon of the Saint (*Ἔχει μὲν ἡ θειοτάτη σου ψυχή*) and the Troparion of the Earthquake *Ὁ ἐπιβλέπων ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν καὶ ποιῶν αὐτὴν τρέμειν* (Psalm 103:32 LXX) substituted in place of the Theotokion. At Matins (§ 2), two canons are appointed: the Canon of the Earthquake in Tone 6 (by Saint Joseph the Hymnographer, with the penitential refrain *Δόξα σοι, ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν, δόξα σοι*) and the second Canon of the Saint in Tone 4 (by Saint Theophanes the Branded, having the acrostic *Μερίς μου, Δημήτριε*); the Troparion of the Earthquake replaces the Theotokion after Ode 3. At the Divine Liturgy (§ 3), the Epistle is 2 Timothy 2:1–10 ("Thou therefore, my son, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus... Endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ") and the Gospel is John 15:17–16:2 ("These things I command you, that ye love one another..."). Sections 4–8 provide detailed rubrics for Saturday and Sunday concurrences.

[^167]: Textual Criticism of the Praises Doxastikon of Saint Demetrios and Violakis's Editorial Defense (Violakis, pp. 204–205, October 26, § 7 note 1). This footnote reproduces in full the crucial critical annotation printed at the foot of pages 204–205 in the 1888 edition: "In the Typikon of Constantine [the Byzantios, Protopsaltes of the Great Church], published in 1851, a note appears here correcting the ending of this Doxastikon [at the Praises: *Τὸν λόγχαις κληρωσάμενον* / 'Pierced by spears'], which reads: 'the protector of the Thessalonians in many and frequent dire perils' (*τὸν ἐν πολλοῖς καὶ πολλάκις κινδύνοις χαλεποῖς τῶν Θεσσαλονικέων προϊστάμενον*), altering it to: 'the protector of all the pious in many and dire perils' (*τὸν ἐν πολλοῖς καὶ... χαλεποῖς πᾶσι τοῖς εὐσεβέσι προϊστάμενον*). But because this correction neither succeeds grammatically, nor is it permitted to alter hymns arbitrarily according to one's liking—especially those in which mention is made of events possessing historical significance—for these reasons it is recommended to the chanter that he preserve with all exactitude the text as it is found originally." George Violakis here establishes a primary methodological principle of Constantinopolitan liturgical editorial practice: ancient hymnographic texts recording historical topoi (in this case, Saint Demetrios's specific historical role as miraculous defender and patron of Thessalonica against barbarian sieges) must not be bowdlerized or universalized to satisfy modern stylistic taste.

[^171]: Synaxis of the Archistrategoi Michael and Gabriel and All the Bodiless Powers, Katavasiai of the Entry, and Festal Propers (Violakis, pp. 206–209, November 8, §§ 1–2). The feast of the Synaxis of the Archistrategoi Michael and Gabriel and all the Heavenly Bodiless Powers is ranked among the major non-dominical feasts of the liturgical year. At Great Vespers (§ 1), 6 festal Prosomoia are sung at "Lord, I have cried" followed by three Old Testament lections: Joshua 5:13–15 (the appearance of the Archistrategos of the Lord's host to Joshua before Jericho); Judges 6:11–24 (the Angel of the Lord calling Gideon); and Isaiah 14:7–20 (the fall of the morning star Lucifer). [^172]: Divine Liturgy of the Bodiless Powers and Sunday Concurrence (Violakis, pp. 208–211, November 8, §§ 3–6). For the Divine Liturgy (§ 3), the Beatitudes assign troparia from Odes 3 and 6 of the second Canon of the Archistrategoi. The appointed lections are: Epistle: Hebrews 2:2–10 (pericope 305, Christ made lower than the angels to taste death for every man); Gospel: Luke 10:16–21 (pericope 51, "I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven"); and the Communion Verse is Psalm 103:4 LXX. When the feast occurs on a Sunday (§§ 4–6), the Resurrection propers take precedence in the first position at Vespers, Matins, and Divine Liturgy: at Vespers, 4 Resurrection and 6 Archangels; at Matins, the Kathismata interleave the Resurrection and festal texts across three stichologiae; at the Divine Liturgy, the Beatitudes take 4 of the Tone and 4 from Ode 6 of Canon 2, while the Epistle is of the feast and the Gospel is of the Sunday.

[^173]: Commemoration of the Holy Martyrs Menas, Victor, Vincent, and Stephanie; Theodore the Studite; John the Merciful; and Nilus the Ascetic (Violakis, pp. 210–213, November 11, §§ 1–3; November 12, § 1). November 11 commemorates the third-century military martyr Saint Menas of Egypt (d. 296), martyred with Victor and Vincent, and Saint Stephanie; combined with the great monastic reformer and confessor Saint Theodore the Studite (d. 826). Under the Constantinopolitan parish rule, when November 11 falls on a weekday (§ 1), both offices are combined according to the Menaion; however, when falling on a Sunday (§§ 2–3), the office of Saint Theodore is deferred to Compline (*Ἡ δὲ τοῦ Ὁσίου Ἀκολουθία ψάλλεται ἐν τοῖς Ἀποδείπνοις*) to allow the full union of the Resurrection and martyr propers at Vespers and Matins. At the Divine Liturgy (§ 3), the Epistle is 2 Corinthians 4:6–15 (pericope 176, "treasure in earthen vessels") and the Gospel is that of the Sunday. November 12 similarly commemorates Saint John the Merciful, Patriarch of Alexandria (d. 619), and Saint Nilus the Ascetic of Sinai (d. ca. 430); on a Sunday, the office of Saint Nilus is likewise transferred to Compline, and the Divine Liturgy follows the exact structure of November 11 §§ 2–3.

[^174]: Feast of Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople, Sunday Concurrence, and Inter-Cohort Boundary (Violakis, pp. 212–215, November 13, §§ 1–5). November 13 marks the feast of Saint John Chrysostom (transferred from the historical date of his repose on September 14 due to the Feast of the Universal Exaltation of the Precious Cross). At Great Vespers (§ 1), the First Stasis of the Psalter (*Blessed is the man*, Pss. 1–3 LXX) is sung; at "Lord, I have cried", 3 Prosomoia are doubled to 6 (*Τὴν χρυσήλατον Σάλπιγγα*), followed by three Old Testament lections (Proverbs 10:7, 6; 3:13–16; 8:6 etc.; Proverbs 10:31–11:12; Wisdom 4:7–15); the Dismissal Troparion is the celebrated hierarchal troparion: *Ἡ τοῦ στόματός σου καθάπερ πυρσὸς ἐκλάμψασα χάρις* ("The grace of thy mouth shining forth like a torch hath enlightened the universe"). At Matins (§ 2), the Prokeimenon is Psalm 48:4 LXX (*Τὸ στόμα μου λαλήσει σοφίαν* / "My mouth shall speak wisdom"), the Gospel is John 10:9–16, and the Praises Doxastikon is *Χρυσέοις ἔπεσι*. At the Divine Liturgy (§ 3), the Epistle is Hebrews 7:26–8:2 (pericope 318, "For such an high priest became us") and the Communion Verse is Psalm 111:6 LXX (*Εἰς μνημόσυνον αἰώνιον ἔσται δίκαιος*). When occurring on a Sunday (§§ 4–5), the Resurrection office is combined with that of the Hierarch. Physical leaf p229 (printed page 214) and facing English leaf p230 (printed page 215) conclude Cohort 23 at the Sunday Matins Kathismata clause: *τὸ Ψαλτήριον καὶ ὁ...* / *the Psalter and the Polyeleos. The Resurrection Kathismata in order;...*, transitioning directly to printed page 216 (physical leaf p231) in Cohort 24.

[^176]: Commemoration of the Holy Apostle and Evangelist Matthew and Sunday Observance (Violakis, pp. 216–219, November 16, §§ 1–3). [^177]: Forefeast of the Entrance of the Most Holy Theotokos, Saints Gregory the Decapolite and Proclus, and Violakis's Critical Erratum on the Forefeast Kathisma (Violakis, pp. 218–221, November 20, §§ 1–4). November 20 commemorates the Forefeast of the Entrance of the Mother of God, joined with Saint Gregory the Decapolite (d. 842) and Saint Proclus, Archbishop of Constantinople and disciple of Chrysostom (d. 446; printed as "Patroclos" in the 1888 edition). [^178]: The Great Feast of the Entrance of the Most Holy Theotokos into the Temple: Vespers, Matins, and Ninth Ode Festal Megalynaria (Violakis, pp. 220–223, November 21, §§ 5–6). November 21 marks the Entry of the Most Holy Theotokos into the Temple, ranked among the Twelve Great Feasts of the liturgical year. At Great Vespers (§ 5), following the First Stasis of the Psalter (*Blessed is the man*, Pss. 1–3 LXX), 6 festal Stichira are sung at "Lord, I have cried" (*Σήμερον πιστοί* and *Τῶν Ἁγίων εἰς Ἅγια*), followed by three Old Testament composite lections: Exodus 40:1–5, 9–10, 16, 34–35 (the erection and consecration of the Tabernacle of Witness and the cloud of the glory of the Lord); 1 Kings 8:1, 3–7, 9–11 (the translation of the Ark of the Covenant into the Holy of Holies of Solomon's Temple); and Ezekiel 43:27–44:4 (the vision of the closed East Gate through which none but the Lord God of Israel enters). At the Aposticha, the Dismissal Troparion *Σήμερον τῆς εὐδοκίας θεοῦ τὸ προοίμιον* ("Today is the prelude of the goodwill of God") is chanted thrice. At Matins (§ 6), the Polyeleos is the Marian Psalm 44 LXX (*Ἐξηρεύξατο ἡ καρδία μου* / "My heart hath poured forth a good word"), the Prokeimenon is Psalm 44:11 LXX (*Ἄκουσον, θύγατερ, καὶ ἴδε* / "Hear, O daughter, and see"), and the Gospel is Luke 1:39–49, 56 (the Visitation to Elizabeth and the Magnificat). At Ode 9, the two festal canons (First Canon in Tone 4 by George of Nicomedia, Second Canon in Tone 1 by Basil of Paganiote) are sung with their distinctive Ninth Ode Megalynaria: the Tone 4 refrain *Ἄγγελοι τὴν Εἴσοδον τῆς Παρθένου ὁρῶντες ἐξεπλήττοντο* ("The Angels, beholding the Entrance of the Virgin, were struck with wonder") and the Tone 1 refrain *Μεγάλυνον ψυχή μου τὴν προσενεχθεῖσαν ἐν τῷ Ναῷ Κυρίου* ("Magnify, O my soul, her who was brought into the Temple of the Lord"). The Katavasia of Ode 9 is *Μυστήριον ξένον* ("A strange and wonderful mystery"), and the Dismissal Troparion is chanted at the end of the Great Doxology.

[^179]: Festal Antiphons of the Divine Liturgy for the Entrance of the Theotokos and Inter-Cohort Boundary (Violakis, pp. 224–225, November 21, § 7). Physical leaf p239 (printed page 224) and facing English leaf p240 (printed page 225) conclude Cohort 24 at the final verse of Antiphon 3, transitioning immediately across the cohort boundary to physical leaf p241 (printed page 226) in Cohort 25 for the Little Entrance with the Gospel, the Introit verse, the Apolytikia, the Kontakion, and the festal Eucharistic lections.

[^182]: Apodosis of the Entrance of the Most Holy Theotokos, Commemoration of the Great-Martyrs Catherine and Mercurius, Sunday Concurrence, and the Nativity Pre-festal Kontakion Rubric (Violakis, pp. 228–233, November 25, §§ 14–19). [^183]: Feast of the Holy Apostle Andrew the First-Called: Weekday Typikon (Violakis, pp. 232–235, November 30, §§ 1–3). [^184]: Feast of the Holy Apostle Andrew the First-Called: Sunday Concurrence (Violakis, pp. 234–235, November 30, §§ 4–5). At Sunday Matins (§ 3), the Litiya of Saint Savvas is performed after Psalm 50 [LXX]; at the Psalter, the first two stichologiai take the Resurrection Kathismata while the third assigns the Kathisma of the Saint; the canons combine the Resurrection Canon with that of the Saint; after Ode 3, the Kontakion, Ikos, and Kathisma of Saint Savvas are chanted; after Ode 6, the Resurrection Kontakion and Ikos are chanted with the Menaion Synaxarion; and the Katavasiai are *Χριστὸς γεννᾶται*. At the Divine Liturgy (§ 4), the Beatitudes assign 4 to the Tone and 4 to Ode 6 of the Saint's canon, with the Epistle of the Saint (Galatians 5:22–6:2, the fruits of the Spirit) read before the Sunday Gospel.

[^187]: Feast of Saint Nicholas the Wonderworker, Archbishop of Myra in Lycia, and Patriarchal Textual Criticism on Nicholas Malaxos (Violakis, pp. 240–243, December 5 § 4 concl.; December 6, §§ 1–3, Note 1). December 6 marks the universal solemnity of Saint Nicholas the Wonderworker, Archbishop of Myra in Lycia (ca. 270–343). At Great Vespers on a weekday (§ 1), following the First Stasis of the Psalter (*Blessed is the man*, Pss. 1–3 LXX), 6 Prosomoia are sung at "Lord, I have cried" to the model melody *Μύροις παροικήσας αἰσθητῶς* ("Having dwelt in Myra in the flesh"), followed by three Old Testament lections (Proverbs 10:7, 6; 3:13–16; 8:6 etc.; Proverbs 10:31–11:12; Wisdom 4:7–15). At Matins (§ 2), after the Polyeleos and the First Antiphon of Tone 4 (*Ἐκ νεότητός μου* / "From my youth"), the Prokeimenon is Psalm 115:6 LXX (*Τίμιος ἐναντίον Κυρίου ὁ θάνατος τῶν ὁσίων αὐτοῦ* / "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His saints"), the Gospel is John 10:9–16, and the canons unite the Theotokion Canon *ᾨδὴν ἐπινίκιον* with the Saint's Canon *Ἀπόρῳ γλώττῃ καὶ χείλεσιν* ("With halting tongue and lips"). Crucially, printed Note 1 on page 240 records a fundamental patriarchal textual decree: the other three Prosomoia composed to the melody *Ποίοις εὐφημιῶν* ("With what garlands of praise") are explicitly prohibited because their author, Nicholas Malaxos (Presbyter of Peloponnesus and Protopresbyter of Nauplion, fl. ca. 1580–1640), had arbitrarily inserted his own compositions into the Venetian printed Menaia without patriarchal synodal sanction. The Holy Synod in Constantinople formally condemned Malaxos as an ecclesiastical innovator (*καινοτόμος*) and permanently banned his interpolated hymns from liturgical cantillation across the Orthodox Church.

[^188]: Feast of Saint Nicholas the Wonderworker: Sunday Concurrence Propers and Liturgical Distribution (Violakis, pp. 242–245, December 6, §§ 4–6). When the feast of Saint Nicholas coincides with a Sunday, the Typikon establishes the full rubrical synthesis between the Resurrectional dominical cursus and the feast of the Hierarch. At Saturday Great Vespers (§ 4), 4 Resurrection Stichira and 6 of Saint Nicholas (*Μύροις παροικήσας*) are chanted at "Lord, I have cried", followed at "Glory" by the Doxastikon of the Saint and at "Both now and ever" by the First Dogmatic Theotokion of the Tone; the Old Testament lections of the Hierarch are read; and at the Aposticha, the Resurrection Stichira are joined with "Glory" of the Saint and the Forefeast Theotokion *Ἀνύμφευτε Παρθένε, πόθεν ἥκεις;* ("O unwedded Virgin, whence art thou come?"). At Sunday Matins (§ 5), following the Polyeleos, the Kathismata are distributed across three stichologiai: at the first two, one Resurrection Kathisma and one of Saint Nicholas with its Theotokion; at the third, the Kathisma of the Saint with its Theotokion. The canons combine the Resurrection Canon with that of the Hierarch; after Ode 3, the Resurrection Kontakion and Ikos are recited plain, followed by the Kathisma and Theotokion of Saint Nicholas; after Ode 6, the Kontakion and Ikos of the Saint are chanted with the Menaion Synaxarion; and the Katavasiai are *Χριστὸς γεννᾶται*. At the Praises, 4 Resurrection Stichira and 4 of the Saint are sung, followed at "Glory" by the Saint's Doxastikon *Σαλπίσωμεν ἐν σάλπιγγι ᾀσμάτων* ("Let us blow the trumpet of praise") and at "Both now and ever" by *Ὑπερευλογημένη* ("Most blessed art Thou, O Virgin Theotokos").

[^189]: Feast of the Conception of Saint Anna, the Mother of the Theotokos, and Dedication of the Church of the Resurrection in Jerusalem (Violakis, pp. 244–245, December 6 § 6 concl.; December 9, §§ 1–3). December 9 celebrates the Conception by Saint Anna of the Most Holy Theotokos, joined with the commemoration of the Dedication (*Enkainia*) of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre (the Anastasis) in Jerusalem. On a weekday (§ 1), both offices are combined according to the Menaion. When December 9 coincides with a Sunday (§§ 2–3), Saturday Great Vespers appoints 6 Resurrection Stichira and 4 of Saint Anna at "Lord, I have cried", followed at "Glory" by *Τὸ ἀπόρρητον τοῖς Ἀγγέλοις* ("That which was inexpressible to the Angels") and at "Both now and ever" by the First Dogmatic Theotokion of the Tone; at the Aposticha, the Resurrection Stichira conclude at "Glory; Both now and ever" with *Σήμερον ἐκ ῥίζης τοῦ Δαβίδ* ("Today from the root of David"); and the Dismissal Troparion of Saint Anna is *Σήμερον τῆς ἀτεκνίας δεσμὰ διαλύονται* ("Today the bonds of barrenness are loosed"). At Sunday Matins (§ 3), the Polyeleos is chanted; the Kathismata interleave 2 of the Resurrection and one of Saint Anna (*Ὁ νέος οὐρανός* / "The new heaven") at the first stichologia, and 2 of the Resurrection and one of Saint Anna (*Ἀναβόησον, Δαυίδ* / "Cry aloud, O David") at the second; the canons unite the Resurrection Canon with that of Saint Anna (*Τὴν σύλληψιν σήμερον* / "Thy conception today"); after Ode 3, the Kathisma *Χορὸς προφητικός* ("The prophetic choir") is sung with the Theotokion *Ἰωακεὶμ ὁ Ἱερεὺς καὶ ἡ Ἄννα* ("Joachim the Priest and Anna"); after Ode 6, the Resurrection Kontakion and Ikos are chanted with the Synaxarion; and the Katavasiai are *Χριστὸς γεννᾶται*. At the Praises, 4 Resurrection Stichira and 4 of Saint Anna (*Πληροφοροῦ, Ἀδάμ* / "Rejoice, O Adam") are sung, with the leaf terminating mid-sentence at "Both now and ever: Most", which resolves seamlessly into Cohort 27 on physical leaf p261.

[^194]: Sunday before the Nativity of Christ (The Holy Fathers, Case 1, §§ 2–3 concluded). Physical leaf p269 (printed page 254) and facing English leaf p270 (printed page 255) conclude Case 1 of the Sunday before the Nativity of Christ (when occurring on December 18 or 19). Physical leaf p279 (printed page 264) and facing English leaf p280 (printed page 265) conclude the Royal Hours of the Nativity. At the Third Hour (§ 3 concl.), the Second Canonarch proclaims the Prophecy (Baruch 3:35–4:4, Christ appearing upon earth and conversing with men) and the Epistle (Galatians 3:23–29, the Law as tutor unto Christ, and adoption as sons through faith), and the Priest reads the Gospel (Luke 2:1–20, the Caesar Augustus census, the manger, and the Angelic Gloria heard by the shepherds). At the Sixth Hour (§ 4), after Psalms 71, 131, and 90 LXX, the idiomela are *Δεῦτε πιστοὶ ἐπαρθῶμεν ἐνθέως* ("Come, ye faithful, let us be inspired divinely"), *Ἄκουε, οὐρανέ* ("Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth"), and *Δεῦτε, χριστοφόροι λαοί* ("Come, ye Christ-bearing peoples"); the Prophecy is Isaiah 7:10–16; 8:1–4, 9–10 (the virgin conceiving Emmanuel), the Epistle is Hebrews 2:11–18 (Christ partaking of flesh and blood to destroy the devil), and the Gospel is Matthew 2:1–12 (the Adoration of the Magi). At the Ninth Hour (§ 5), after Psalms 109, 110, and 85 LXX, the idiomela are *Ἐξεπλήττετο ὁ Ἡρώδης* ("Herod was struck with amazement") and *Ὅτε Ἰωσήφ, Παρθένε* ("When Joseph, O Virgin"); then the Canonarch stands in the midst of the nave facing east and solemnly chants the celebrated idiomelon *Σήμερον γεννᾶται ἐκ Παρθένου ὁ δρακὶ τὴν πᾶσαν ἔχων κτίσιν* ("Today He Who holds all creation in the hollow of His hand is born of a Virgin") in Gospel recitative style thrice, continuing with the strophes, repeating thrice *Προσκυνοῦμέν σου τὴν γέννησιν, Χριστέ* ("We worship Thy Nativity, O Christ"), and once *Δεῖξον ἡμῖν καὶ τὰ θεῖά σου Θεοφάνεια* ("Show us also Thy divine Theophany"), whereupon the choirs repeat the idiomelon melodiously; the Prophecy is Isaiah 9:6–7 (Unto us a Child is born), the Epistle is Hebrews 2:1–10 (Jesus crowned with glory and honor), and the Gospel is Matthew 2:13–23 (the Flight into Egypt and Slaughter of the Holy Innocents). In Note 3, Violakis explains that historically the Typika were read after the Ninth Hour, but in modern practice are omitted to transition directly to Great Vespers with the Liturgy of Saint Basil the Great.

On Monday evening and Tuesday morning (Dec 25–26, § 36), Vespers, Matins, and Divine Liturgy for the Synaxis of the Most Holy Theotokos are celebrated as prescribed in Situation One §§ 9–10; the Epistle is Hebrews 2:11–18 (*Ὁ ἁγιάζων καὶ οἱ ἁγιαζόμενοι* / "Both He that sanctifieth and they who are sanctified are all of one"), and the Gospel is Matthew 2:13–23 (*Ἀναχωρησάντων τῶν Μάγων* / "And when the wise men had departed"). Paragraphs 37–38 govern the case where the Sunday after the Nativity (Holy Ancestors: David the King, Joseph the Betrothed, and James the Brother of the Lord) coincides with the Apodosis of the Feast on Sunday, December 31. On Saturday evening (§ 37), Great Vespers at "Lord, I have cried" features 10 Stichira (3 Resurrectional, 4 Festal Idiomela *Δεῦτε ἀγαλλιασώμεθα*, and 3 of the Ancestors of God); "Glory" (*Μνήμην ἐπιτελοῦμεν*); "Both now and ever" (*Αὐγούστου μοναρχήσαντος*); Entrance, *Φῶς ἱλαρόν*, Prokeimenon; Aposticha Resurrectional with "Glory" of the Ancestors (*Ἱερέων μνήμη*), "Both now and ever" (*Σπηλαίῳ παρῴκησας*); Dismissal Troparia: Resurrectional, of the Ancestors (*Εὐαγγελίζου, Ἰωσήφ*), and of the Feast (*Ἡ γέννησίς σου*). On Sunday Matins (§ 38), after Psalm 50 [LXX], the Triadic Canon and Triadic hymns (*Ἄξιόν ἐστιν*) are sung, followed by the Trisagion Prayers, Troparion *Ἡ γέννησίς σου*, and Hexapsalmos; "God is the Lord", Troparia as at Vespers; Psalter and Amomos (Kathisma 17 / Psalm 118 LXX); Resurrectional Kathismata with Festal Kathismata instead of Theotokia; Evlogitaria, Hypakoe, Anavathmoi of the Tone, Prokeimenon; Canons of the Resurrection, of the Feast (*Δόξα σοι ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν*), and of Joseph the Betrothed (*Χριστοῦ θεράπων μακάριε*); after Ode 3, Resurrectional Kontakion and Ikos plain, Kathisma *Πατρὸς ὡς ἀληθῶς*, "Both now and ever" *Χορὸς τῶν Προφητῶν*; after Ode 6, Kontakion and Ikos of the Sunday after the Nativity, Menologion and Synaxarion; double Katavasiai of the Nativity (*Ἔσωσε λαόν* and *Στείβει θαλάσσης*); Morning Gospel order; Ode 9 from both festal canons with their Megalynaria and both Katavasiai of Ode 9; Exapostilaria of the Resurrection, Ancestors, and Feast; Praises with 4 Resurrectional and 4 Festal Stichira; "Glory" (*Αἷμα καὶ πῦρ*), "Both now and ever" (*Ὑπερευλογημένη*), and Great Doxology.

[^212]: Divine Liturgy of the Sunday after the Nativity and Apodosis (§ 39); Situation Five: Nativity falling on Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday (§ 40); and Sunday after the Nativity during the Afterfeast (Saturday Vespers § 41 and Sunday Matins § 42). Physical leaf p305 (printed page 290) and facing English leaf p306 (printed page 291) conclude the Liturgy for Situation Four and open Situation Five (Ε΄). At the Divine Liturgy of the Sunday after the Nativity and Apodosis (§ 39), the Antiphons of the Feast are sung with the Second Antiphon refrain *Ὁ ἐκ Παρθένου τεχθείς* ("Who wast born of a Virgin"); Entrance Verse of the Feast with the Sunday addition *Ὁ ἀναστὰς ἐκ νεκρῶν* ("Who art risen from the dead"); Dismissal Troparia: Resurrectional, Festal (*Ἡ γέννησίς σου*), Ancestors (*Εὐαγγελίζου, Ἰωσήφ*), and Temple Patron; Kontakion *Ἡ Παρθένος σήμερον*; Trisagion Hymn; Epistle (2 Timothy 4:5–8) and Gospel (Mark 1:1–8) of the Sunday before Theophany; at "Especially", the Festal Megalynarion and Heirmos of Ode 9 *Μεγάλυνον ἡ ψυχή μου . . . Στέργειν μὲν ἡμᾶς*; Communion Verse Psalm 110:9 LXX (*Λύτρωσιν ἀπέστειλε* / "The Lord hath sent redemption unto His people"); Dismissal Troparion *Ἡ γέννησίς σου*, Dismissal. Situation Five (§ 40) governs Christmas occurring on Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday: the Paramony Royal Hours, Great Vespers, and Liturgy of Saint Basil the Great, as well as the festal services and the Synaxis of the Theotokos, follow Situation One §§ 1–11. Paragraphs 41–42 detail the celebration of the Sunday after the Nativity when it occurs on an intermediate day of the afterfeast (between Dec 26 and 31). On Saturday evening (§ 41), Great Vespers at "Lord, I have cried" has 10 Stichira (4 Resurrectional, 3 Festal Idiomela *Δεῦτε ἀγαλλιασώμεθα*, 3 of the Ancestors of God); "Glory" (*Μνήμην ἐπιτελοῦμεν*); "Both now and ever": First Theotokion Dogmatikon of the Tone (distinct from Situation Four, where the festal Doxastikon is sung); Entrance, *Φῶς ἱλαρόν*, Prokeimenon; Aposticha Resurrectional with "Glory" of the Ancestors (*Ἱερέων μνήμη*), "Both now and ever" (*Χορεύουσιν Ἄγγελοι*); Dismissal Troparia: Resurrectional, Ancestors (*Εὐαγγελίζου, Ἰωσήφ*), Festal (*Ἡ γέννησίς σου*), Dismissal. On Sunday Matins (§ 42), after Psalm 50 [LXX], Triadic Canon and Triadic hymns (*Ἄξιόν ἐστιν*), Trisagion Prayers, Troparion *Ἡ γέννησίς σου*, Hexapsalmos; "God is the Lord", Troparia as at Vespers; Psalter and Amomos; Resurrectional Kathismata with afterfeast Kathismata instead of Theotokia; Evlogitaria, Hypakoe, Anavathmoi of the Tone, Prokeimenon; Canons of the Resurrection and of Joseph the Betrothed (the festal canon being omitted here); after Ode 3, Resurrectional Kontakion and Ikos plain, Kathisma *Πατρὸς ὡς ἀληθῶς*...

[^213]: Situation Five Concluded: Matins and Divine Liturgy of the Sunday after the Nativity (§§ 42 concl., 43); Month of January: January 1, Circumcision of our Lord Jesus Christ and Commemoration of Saint Basil the Great (Vespers § 1 and opening of Matins § 2). Physical leaf p307 (printed page 292) and facing English leaf p308 (printed page 293) conclude the five Situations of the Nativity and begin the Month of January. Matins of the Sunday after the Nativity under Situation Five (§ 42 concl.) concludes with Kathisma "Both now and ever" *Χορὸς τῶν Προφητῶν*; after Ode 6: Kontakion of the Sunday after the Nativity (*Εὐφροσύνης σήμερον* / "Of joy today") and Ikos (*Ἀπορρήτῳ βουλῇ* / "By ineffable counsel"), Menologion and Synaxarion; Katavasiai *Ἔσωσε λαόν* (single canon only); Morning Gospel order; Magnificat (*Τὴν τιμιωτέραν* is sung); Exapostilaria of Resurrection, Ancestors, and Feast; Praises with 4 Resurrectional and 4 Festal Stichira (*Εὐφραίνεσθε, δίκαιοι*); "Glory" (*Αἷμα καὶ πῦρ*), "Both now and ever" (*Ὑπερευλογημένη*), Great Doxology, and *Σήμερον σωτηρία*. At the Divine Liturgy (§ 43): Typika and 4 Beatitudes of the Tone, and 4 from Ode 6 of Canon of the Betrothed; Entrance with Resurrectional Dismissal Troparion, *Ἡ γέννησίς σου*, *Εὐαγγελίζου, Ἰωσήφ*, Temple Patron, Kontakion *Ἡ Παρθένος σήμερον*; Epistle Galatians 1:11–19, Gospel Matthew 2:13–23; at "Especially": *Ἄξιόν ἐστιν* (normal Megalynarion, since it is an intermediate day and not the Apodosis); Communion Verse Psalm 148:1 LXX (*Αἰνεῖτε τὸν Κύριον* / "Praise the Lord from the heavens"); *Εἴδομεν τὸ φῶς*, Dismissal. Formal rubric closes: *End of the five Situations of the Feast of the Nativity of Christ.* The Month of January opens on January 1 with the Circumcision of Christ and Saint Basil the Great. At Vespers (§ 1): Introductory Psalm [Ps. 103 LXX], First Stasis of the First Kathisma [Ps. 1–3 LXX]; at "Lord, I have cried", 6 Stichira (2 Festal Idiomela repeating the first, 3 Prosomoia of Saint Basil); "Glory" of the Saint (*Σοφίας ἐραστής*); "Both now and ever" (*Συγκαταβαίνων ὁ Σωτήρ*); Entrance, *Φῶς ἱλαρόν*, Prokeimenon of the day, 3 Old Testament Readings (Genesis 17:1–14; Proverbs 8:22–30; Proverbs 10:31–11:12); Aposticha: 3 Idiomela of the Saint, "Glory" (*Ὁ τὴν χάριν τῶν θαυμάτων*), "Both now and ever" (*Οὐκ ἐπῃσχύνθη ὁ πανάγαθος Θεός*); Dismissal Troparion of the Saint (*Εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν*), then "Glory... Both now and ever...": of the Feast once (*Μορφὴν ἀναλλοιώτως*), and the festal Dismissal (*Ὁ ἐν τῇ ὀγδόῃ ἡμέρᾳ σαρκὶ περιτμηθῆναι καταδεξάμενος διὰ τὴν ἡμῶν σωτηρίαν Χριστὸς ὁ ἀληθινὸς Θεὸς ἡμῶν...*). At Matins (§ 2): after Psalm 50 [LXX], Lite of the Saint; Trisagion Prayers, Troparion *Μορφὴν ἀναλλοιώτως*, Hexapsalmos.

[^214]: January 1 Matins Concluded (§ 2) and Complete Festal Megalynaria of Ode 9 for the Circumcision of Christ and Saint Basil the Great. Physical leaf p309 (printed page 294) and facing English leaf p310 (printed page 295) conclude Matins for January 1. At "God is the Lord": Dismissal Troparion of Saint Basil twice, and of the Feast once; Psalter of the day and Polyeleos; Kathismata in order; Anavathmoi: First Antiphon of Tone 4 (*Ἐκ νεότητός μου*); Prokeimenon: Violakis notes *Εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν ἐξῆλθεν ὁ φθόγγος αὐτοῦ* [Ps. 18:5 LXX], adding the critical rubrical note that the Menaion and standard liturgical sources indicate *Τὸ στόμα μου λαλήσει σοφίαν* ("My mouth shall speak wisdom", Psalm 48:4 LXX); *Πᾶσα πνοή*; Morning Gospel (John 10:1–9, from November 13); Psalm 50 [LXX] plain; "Glory": *Ταῖς τοῦ Ἱεράρχου*; "Both now and ever": *Ταῖς τῆς Θεοτόκου*; Verse Psalm 50:3 LXX (*Ἐλέησόν με, ὁ Θεός*); Idiomelon *Ἐξεχύθη ἡ χάρις ἐν χείλεσί σου* (Tone 6); Canon of the Feast *Δεῦτε λαοί* with Verse *Δόξα σοι ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν*, and Canon of Saint Basil *Σοῦ τὴν φωνήν* with Verse *Ἅγιε τοῦ Θεοῦ*; after Ode 3, Kathismata of Saint Basil and the Feast; after Ode 6, Kontakion and Ikos of Saint Basil, and Menologion; double Katavasiai of Theophany (*Βυθοῦ ἀνεκάλυψε πυθμένα* and *Στείβει θαλάσσης*); Ode 9 of both Feast and Saint sung with their respective Megalynaria. The leaf provides the complete text of the Megalynaria for Ode 9: for Canon 1 (Circumcision), 5 refrains (including the Menaion addition in brackets: "Today the Master is circumcised in the flesh, fulfilling the Law as an infant"); and for Canon 2 (Saint Basil), 4 refrains (including the Menaion additions in brackets: "Magnify, O my soul, the most bright luminary of the universe" and "Magnify, O my soul, the adorner of the Church of Christ"). The footnote preserves Violakis's editorial asterisk indicating that these bracketed refrains are commonly chanted in contemporary practice.
